bridge: Builds on P06 programs, M01 binary and L02 the shell. Use a local C compiler from the linked CS50 setup, not a production machine configuration change.
teaching:
C source is text. A compiler translates it, and a linker resolves references to libraries to produce an executable. A syntax error stops translation; a runtime error happens after the program starts. Read compiler diagnostics rather than treating successful compilation as evidence of correct behaviour.

A type determines representation and permitted operations. Integer sizes depend on the type and implementation; do not assume every int is the same size everywhere. sizeof reports bytes for this implementation. Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo one more than its maximum value; signed overflow is undefined behaviour, so it is not a portable wraparound technique.

Bytes have addresses and an order in memory. Endianness concerns the ordering of bytes within a multi-byte value, not the order in which you write ordinary decimal digits. Compile with warnings enabled and keep examples small enough to trace. Undefined behaviour can appear to work in one build, then change under optimisation; a single output is not a language guarantee.
explanation: UINT_MAX is the implementation's largest unsigned int. Adding unsigned 1 wraps to zero by the language rule. The %zu conversion matches sizeof's size_t type. Replacing the unsigned variable with a maximum signed int and overflowing it would remove the portable guarantee; do not infer signed behaviour from this result.
exercise: Compile the supplied program and record compiler version, command, warnings and output. Draw how the number 0x0102 would occupy two bytes under little-endian and big-endian conventions. Do not claim sizeof(int) is universal.
solution: Little-endian: lower address 02 then 01; big-endian: 01 then 02. Unsigned wrap prints zero. The observed size belongs to the recorded platform.
challenge: Explain each stage from source to execution. In an explicitly eight-bit unsigned model calculate 250+10; then explain why that result cannot automatically be asserted for signed char in a real C program.
challenge_solution: The model gives 260 mod256=4. Signedness and representation rules differ; signed overflow is not defined as modular arithmetic. A full answer separates the mathematical model, C guarantees and observed implementation.
